recipe: Store authentication tokens in cookies configured with the HttpOnly attribute rather than in localStorage, so client-side JavaScript cannot read them directly, reducing XSS token-theft risk.
trigger_condition: You are implementing client-side authentication in a React SPA and need to decide where to persist the user's JWT or session token.
evidence: Opting to store tokens in cookies, configured with the `HttpOnly` attribute, can enhance security as they are inaccessible to client-side JavaScript.

recipe: Sanitize all user inputs before rendering them in the DOM to reduce the risk of Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities.
trigger_condition: Your React application displays user-supplied content (e.g., comments, names, descriptions) in the UI.
evidence: One key strategy is to sanitize all user inputs before displaying them in the application.

recipe: Persist the authentication token in localStorage or sessionStorage instead of keeping it only in application state, so the user's authenticated session survives a page refresh.
trigger_condition: You are storing a JWT in React application state and notice the user loses their login after refreshing the browser tab.
evidence: That is why tokens need to be stored in a cookie or `localStorage/sessionStorage`.

recipe: For user state management, use react-query-auth if you are already using react-query, or fall back to React context with hooks or a third-party state management library.
trigger_condition: You need to make the authenticated user object globally accessible across your React application.
evidence: If you are already using `react-query`, you can use [react-query-auth](https://github.com/alan2207/react-query-auth) library for handling user state which will handle all the things for you after you provide it some configuration. Otherwise, you can use react context + hooks, or some 3rd party state management library.

recipe: Implement role-based access control by defining specific roles (e.g., USER, ADMIN) and associating each role with a set of permissions, then gate UI features and API calls on the user's role.
trigger_condition: Your application has multiple user roles with different levels of access to features or resources.
evidence: In a role-based authorization model, access to resources is determined by defining specific roles and associating them with permissions.

recipe: When RBAC is too coarse (e.g., you need to allow only the owner of a specific resource to perform an operation), switch to permission-based access control and pass a policy check to your authorization component.
trigger_condition: You need fine-grained, per-resource permission checks that go beyond simple role assignment, such as restricting deletion of a comment to its author.
evidence: Permission-Based Access Control (PBAC) offers a more flexible solution, particularly in scenarios where access permissions need to be finely tuned based on specific criteria

recipe: Wrap protected UI in an RBAC component: pass allowed roles for basic role checks, or pass a policy function for stricter, condition-based protection.
trigger_condition: You are building a component that should only be visible or interactive to users with certain roles or permissions.
evidence: For RBAC protection, you can use the RBAC component by passing allowed roles to it. On the other hand, if you need more strict protection, you can pass policies check to it.
